text: Morris Steinberg (DEM) and Isaac Glanzer (REP) are political figures associated with Palm Tree. Palm Tree is a town coterminous with the village of Kiryas Joel, which is inhabited by the Satmar Hasidic community and was previously part of the municipality of Monroe. The population of Palm Tree was 32,954 according to the 2020 census. The town of Palm Tree, comprising the entirety of Kiryas Joel, was officially established on January 1, 2019. Prior to 2019, the area underwent several geographic and name changes: until 1764, it was part of an enlarged Goshen, which was then divided, with Palm Tree joining Cornwall; by 1799, Cornwall was split, and Palm Tree became part of the town of Cheesekook (later renamed Smithfield or Southfield), which in 1808 became Monroe, either in honor of James Monroe or a local family. In 1974, Satmar rebbe Joel Teitelbaum founded the Kiryas Joel community, and in 1976, it was incorporated as a village in his honor as a semi-rural retreat for his Brooklyn-based community. As the population grew, zoning conflicts with Monroe arose, leading to a referendum on November 7, 2017, which passed overwhelmingly and resulted in the split from Monroe and the creation of Palm Tree, coterminous with Kiryas Joel. On June 14, 2018, special legislation was passed to move the official founding date forward by one year, signed by Governor Andrew Cuomo on July 1. The town became official on January 1, 2019, with officials elected in November 2018 being sworn in on that date. No candidates ran for town justice in 2018 or 2019; however, two non-resident lawyers were elected in the November 2019 elections through a write-in campaign supported by the leadership of the majority faction, as New York law normally requires town justices to be residents, but the town amended its laws to allow non-resident justices. In the same election, residents voted for a single consolidated town-village government to be governed as a village rather than a town. The name "Palm Tree" is a calque of Teitelbaum, meaning "date palm" from "teitel" (date) and "baum" (tree). According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the town has a total area of 1.5 square miles (3.9 km²), with only a small portion—specifically a duck pond called "Forest Road Lake"—covered in water. Palm Tree began with a 2019 founding population of 26,905, but since it shares the same boundaries as Kiryas Joel, its pre-incorporation demographics are known. As of the 2000 census, there were 13,138 people, 2,229 households, and 2,137 families in the village, with a population density of 11,962.2 inhabitants per square mile (4,618.6/km²) and 2,233 housing units at an average density of 2,033.2 units per square mile (785.0 units/km²). The racial composition was 99.02% White, 0.21% African American, 0.02% Asian, 0.12% from other races, and 0.63% from two or more races; Hispanic or Latino of any race made up 0.93%. Kiryas Joel had the highest percentage of people reporting Hungarian ancestry in the U.S., at 18.9% in 2000; 3% were Israeli, 2% Romanian, 1% Polish, and 1% European. In 2000, 6.3% of residents spoke only English at home, one of the lowest in the U.S., while 91.5% spoke Yiddish and 2.3% spoke Hebrew; 46% of Yiddish speakers spoke English "not well" or "not at all," and overall, 46% of residents spoke English "not well" or "not at all" when including those who primarily spoke Hebrew or European languages. There were 2,229 households, 79.5% of which had children under 18, 93.2% were married couples living together, 1.6% had a female householder with no husband, and 4.1% were non-families; 2.8% were made up of individuals, and 2.1% had someone living alone aged 65 or older. The average household size was 5.74, and the average family size was 5.84. The population was very young: 57.5% under 18, 17.2% aged 18–24, 16.5% aged 25–44, 7.2% aged 45–64, and 1.6% aged 65 or older; the median age was 15. For every 100 females, there were 116.3 males, and for every 100 females aged 18 and over, there were 118.0 males. The village follows strict Jewish customs, and its welcome sign (installed in 2010) asks visitors to dress conservatively and maintain gender separation in public areas, though the sign states there are no consequences for violating these guidelines.
